name: AZD6234
lead: AZD6234 is an investigational long-acting selective amylin receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes, given by subcutaneous injection. [1][2]

Amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that acts centrally to promote satiety. The first amylin-based drug, pramlintide, found limited use as an add-on to insulin, and longer-acting analogues are now being developed for weight loss. [1][2] No results from AZD6234 trials have been published in the sources reviewed here; its evidence is limited to early-phase registrations, with phase 3 trials registered from 2026. [3][4][5]

paras: Reviews describe amylin receptors as heterodimers of the calcitonin receptor and receptor activity-modifying proteins, a structure that has guided the design of newer long-acting analogues. Amylin agonists act centrally to induce satiety and slow postprandial glucagon release. [1] A narrative review of amylin analogues for weight loss summarises experimental and early-phase clinical data across the class. [2]

Phase 1 studies have examined single and repeat dosing in overweight or obese participants, renal impairment, and relative bioavailability of subcutaneous formulations. [6][7][8][9] AZD6234 is also being tested in combination with AZD9550, a GLP-1/glucagon agonist, in a phase 2 weight-loss trial. [10]

Phase 3 trials registered in 2026 cover obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes (2,500 participants), obesity with type 2 diabetes (1,500), use as an adjunct to incretin-based therapies (500), and a further weight-management study (330). [3][4][5][11] Results have not been reported.

timeline.event: Phase 3 trials registered in obesity and type 2 diabetes. [3][4][5]

quick.overview:
AZD6234 is an experimental injectable amylin agonist from AstraZeneca being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Phase 3 trials were registered in 2026, but no efficacy results have been published.
quick.mechanism: It mimics amylin, a satiety hormone that acts on the brain and slows glucagon release after meals. It is also being tested together with AZD9550.
quick.risks: Safety is being assessed in phase 1 and 3 studies; no published adverse-event data were found. It is not approved.
